children.text: Will Dyson is The Performance Consultant. His work combines doctoral training in molecular and structural biology with postgraduate study in performance nutrition and applied coaching practice.
Sweetness as a culinary tool
Sweetness carries an unusual amount of moral baggage in fitness culture.
Sweet foods are often associated with rewards, "cheat meals", weakness or evidence of poor discipline, making it difficult to use sweetness
intelligently

. People either remove it completely or consume it reactively after several days of trying not to think about it which, if you're a client of mine, will know is the complete opposite of what we want to do if we like a food or flavour.

Sweetness is simply one component of flavour. It can make fruit, yogurt and oats more satisfying. It can soften the acidity of tomatoes, balance the bitterness of cocoa and moderate an aggressive chilli sauce. Used carefully, it can improve a savoury recipe without making the finished meal taste conventionally sweet.
What creates sweet taste?

Human sweet taste is principally associated with the T1R2/T1R3 receptor complex, which responds to sugars and a range of other sweet-tasting compounds. Sweetness is therefore associated with carbohydrate and energy, but it is
not

a direct or quantifiable measurement of either. For instance, starches such as rice, oats, bread and potatoes provide carbohydrate without tasting intensely sweet, while berries and non-nutritive sweeteners provide sweetness with little or no energy.

This is important for athletes. Despite the cacophony of self-proclaimed social media "experts" proclaiming that your cravings are directly linked to nutritional deficiencies, a craving for sweet food cannot tell you
how much
glycogen
is present in your muscle; nor is a sweet-tasting food an automatically effective recovery meal. Conversely, the presence of
sugar
does not make a food nutritionally inappropriate.

A brief rant on the "evils" of sugar... It pains me to no end to say that last week I waited 5 minutes to grab my protein yogurts from Aldi because two people were deliberating whether or not the 3-4 grams of sugar per 100 g in a protein yogurt was worth it for what is an excellent food choice. I'm confident that, given there were other much higher calorie, sugar-containing and more obesigenic ingredients in their trolley that their reasons were not medical (i.e. diabetes), and while I have no doubt that they are health-conscious and well-intentioned; it was poignant reminder of just how far social media has (wrongly) influenced our behaviours. Without going too off piste, just because a food has sugars included in it does not make it "unhealthy".
Carbohydrate availability (how much glycogen we have) remains relevant to training
performance
and
recovery

, particularly when training volume or intensity is high. The required amount depends on the athlete, the session and the broader programme, where sweetness is one potential delivery format, not the physiological target itself.
Ingredients that contribute sweetness
Obvious sources include sugar, honey, maple syrup, syrups and sweeteners. Plenty of minimally processed foods also provide useful sweetness:
Ripe bananas, mangoes, grapes, apples and stone fruits
Berries and cooked fruit
Dates, raisins and other dried fruit
Milk and yoghurt through lactose
Sweet potatoes, carrots, squash, peas and sweetcorn
Onions and garlic, particularly after browning or slow cooking
Tomato products, which contain both sweetness and acidity

Cooking can concentrate water-soluble sugars and generate caramelised or roasted aromas which add additional and unique flavour bonus points, demonstrating the versatility of sweet foods. This is why roasted carrots and slowly cooked onions taste markedly sweeter than their raw equivalents, even when no sugar has been added.
Sweetness as balance
Sweetness is especially useful in meals dominated by bitterness or acidity.
Cocoa, coffee, certain protein powders and some high-protein yoghurts can produce a
bitter
or astringent finish. Berries add
acidity
. Combining all of these in one bowl can create an impressive nutritional label but an unpleasant breakfast.

A small amount of sweetness - such as via a drizzle of honey or a ripe banana - suppresses some of the harshness, mellowing the bitter and sour/acidic tones, helping the dish come together. The required quantity is often modest because the objective is
balance

rather than dessert-level sweetness. Additionally, taste-mixture research shows that sweetness can be a strong suppressor of other taste qualities, although the size of the effect depends on concentration and context.
Sweetness can also improve
savoury
food:
A small amount of honey can round a sharp mustard dressing.
Sugar can soften an excessively acidic tomato sauce (think ketchup).
Mango or pineapple can balance chilli heat or salty soy sauce (think jerk chicken and mango).
Roasted squash can provide contrast in a bitter kale salad.
A little maple syrup can make miso-coated vegetables substantially more appealing.
The "correct"
amount
often is often imperceptible, where you should notice that the meal tastes more
complete
, rather than identifying sugar as a dominant flavour.
Composite coaching case: if your protein bowl tastes “too healthy”
A client combined low-fat Greek yogurt, chocolate whey, cocoa powder, oats and frozen raspberries.

On paper, it was an efficient and nutritionally-excellent breakfast, but In practice, it tasted sour, bitter and chalky. The client assumed the problem was the yogurt and began looking for a more processed protein snack.
The problem was the
balance
The revised bowl used ripe banana for
sweetness
, a pinch of salt to soften the cocoa’s
bitterness
and enough oats or cereal to provide contrast in
texture,
with an optional 5-10 grams of honey available as an adjustable finish in case more sweetness was needed to moderate.
The breakfast now contained sweetness from fruit, sourness from yogurt and berries, bitterness from cocoa, salt in a supporting role and some savoury depth from the dairy protein.
Example Recipe: Cocoa Cherry Recovery Bowl
Makes one substantial serving
Ingredients
250 g fat-free Greek yogurt or Skyr
20-30 g Chocolate or Vanilla Protein Powder
40-60 g Oats, Cereal or Granola (
scaled to training demand
100 g Cherries or Berries
½ ripe Banana (
mashed
1 tsp Cocoa Powder
A small pinch of Salt
Cinnamon
1 tsp Honey or Maple Syrup (
optional
Method
Mix the yogurt, protein powder, mashed banana, cocoa and salt.
Taste before adding further sweetness.
Add the fruit and oats or cereal.
Use honey or maple syrup to moderate if the bowl tastes too sour or bitter.
*If it becomes cloying, add more berries, a spoonful of plain yoghurt or a small amount of cocoa.
For post-training use, scale the oats, cereal, fruit or honey according to needs.

*I would encourage you to at least once play around with making the dish too sour... neutralise with sweetness... take it to too sweet... neutralise with sour... etc. so you gain an appreciation for how to moderate and use flavour effectively

The banana provides sweetness and body. Salt reduces bitterness. Cherries or berries supply acidity. Cocoa contributes bitterness and roasted aroma. The result has contrast rather than relying on sweetness alone - something many would assume just by reading the title.
What does a sweet craving mean?
Sweet cravings are often interpreted too confidently.
They are sometimes presented as proof of magnesium deficiency, chromium deficiency, low glycogen or “sugar addiction”. A craving cannot diagnose any of these conditions. In fact, the
only
taste we have a physiologically pre-disposed sensitivity to in this sense is
salt
, due to its role in cardiovascular function.
Acute sleep restriction can alter hunger and food reward. In one controlled
study
, sleep restriction increased
ghrelin

and snack intake, with much of the additional energy coming from carbohydrate-rich foods. Other experimental work indicates that caloric deprivation can heighten attention and reward responses to food cues.

body.quote: Ghrelin is a peptide hormone produced mainly by the stomach that stimulates appetite, increases food intake, and promotes fat storage. Widely known as the "hunger hormone," its levels surge when your stomach is empty to signal your brain it's time to eat, and drop after a meal.

children.text: That does not mean
every
craving is caused by poor sleep or under-fuelling.
Longer dietary interventions

sometimes even show reductions in food cravings during energy restriction, illustrating that the response is not uniform. Food access, learned habits, dietary rules and repeated exposure all contribute.
When sweet cravings become persistent, we assess the broader pattern:
Is total energy intake appropriate for the
training load
Are carbohydrate-rich foods concentrated into a
narrow part
of the day?
Are meals being
skipped
during busy work periods?
Is the
post-training
meal sufficiently large if this is a key hunger driver?
Has
sleep
been poor?
Have sweet foods been
labelled
completely off-limits?
Is the craving occurring at a
repeated time and location
, regardless of hunger?
Repeated exposure
also influences perception. In a
five-month trial
, lowering simple-sugar intake increased perceived sweet
intensity
, although it did not reliably change
pleasantness
. The same food can therefore begin to taste sweeter after dietary exposure changes, but preference does not necessarily follow in sync.
Sweetness and sustainable nutrition
Learning to use sweetness removes the false dichotomy between joyless food and uncontrolled indulgence.

An intentional amount of sugar, honey or ripe fruit can save a high-protein breakfast, increase vegetable intake and make a lower-energy sauce substantially more satisfying. Its contribution should be judged in the context of the full meal and the full diet.

Performance nutrition becomes more sustainable when sweetness is planned, portioned and its role is understood. Treating it as contraband only makes it more psychologically conflicting. Treating it as one adjustable part of flavour provides considerably more control.

children.text: Will Dyson is The Performance Consultant. His work combines doctoral training in molecular and structural biology with postgraduate study in performance nutrition and applied coaching practice.

Protein timing receives a disproportionate amount of attention. For most trained people, the first priority is still the amount of high-quality protein consumed across the full day. Distribution becomes useful after that daily target is consistently met.
Start with the daily target

A large meta-analysis found that gains in fat-free mass during resistance training were not meaningfully improved beyond an average intake of approximately 1.6 g of protein per kilogram of body mass per day. This is a population estimate, not a rigid ceiling. Energy restriction, very high training volumes, food preference and individual tolerance can justify a higher target.
For an 80 kg athlete, 1.6 g/kg provides 128 g of protein per day. Establishing that intake consistently is likely to matter more than whether one meal contains 30 g or 35 g.

body.heading: Set the day before optimising each meal
body.label: Practical starting point

children.text: Then distribute it deliberately

Once the daily total is secure, dividing protein across three to five meals is a sensible approach. A practical target is approximately 0.3 to 0.5 g/kg per meal. Four meals at 0.4 g/kg would provide 1.6 g/kg across the day while giving each meal enough protein to stimulate muscle protein synthesis in most adults.

body.caption: Example protein distribution using four meals at approximately 0.4 g/kg per meal.

children.text: The meal around training is part of the day

Resistance exercise increases the muscle response to protein for many hours. There is no need to treat the post-training period as a narrow emergency window. A protein-containing meal within a few hours before or after training is generally sufficient, provided the wider daily intake is appropriate.

body.quote: Protein distribution should make the daily target easier to achieve, not make eating more complicated.

children.text: How to apply this without overengineering it

Choose a daily target that fits the training phase. Divide it between the number of meals you can repeat reliably. Anchor each meal with a recognisable protein source, then adjust portions using training performance, appetite, gastrointestinal comfort and body-composition progress.
A plan is only useful when it survives work, family meals and changes to the training week. The objective is a repeatable structure with enough flexibility to remain accurate when real life changes.
